title: 論語 顏淵第十二
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 12, 〈顏淵〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 12 of the Analects, 顏淵 Yán Yuān, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Yan Yuan, the disciple the Master loved best. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book is made mostly of questions and answers, and the same few questions come round again and again from different askers: what humaneness is (Yan Yuan, Zhonggong, Sima Niu and Fan Chi each get a different answer, 12.1–12.3, 12.22), what government is (Zigong, Duke Jing of Qi, Zizhang, and the powerful minister Ji Kangzi, who also asks what to do about thieves, 12.17–12.19), how to exalt virtue and see through delusion (12.10, 12.21). Among them are some of the most quoted lines in the whole collection: the rule not to lay on others what you would not want yourself (12.2), Zixia's comfort to a man without brothers that everyone within the four seas is his brother (12.5), the answer that a people without good faith cannot stand (12.7), the lord being a lord and the son a son (12.11), and the virtue of those above as wind over grass (12.19). 12.15 repeats a saying already met in Book 6. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
顔淵問仁。
子曰：「
克己復禮為仁。
一日克己復禮，
天下歸仁焉。
為仁由己，
而由人乎哉？」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l:
Yan Yuan asked about humaneness.
The Master said: “Overcoming the self and going back to the rites is the practice of humaneness.
For one day overcome the self and go back to the rites,
and the world will grant you humaneness.
The practice of humaneness comes from oneself —
does it come from others?”
sentences.i: Yan Yuan asked about humaneness. The Master said: “To master the self and come back to the rites — that is the work of humaneness. Let a man do this for just one day, and the whole world will allow that he is humane. It starts from you; how could it start from anyone else?”
sentences.n: The book is named 顏淵 from its opening words; Zhu Xi's heading counts twenty-four chapters. 克己 and 復禮 are two verb–object pairs, 'overcome self' and 'return to the rites'; together they are the subject, and 為仁 is the predicate, 'is to practise humaneness' (為 wéi). 一日 'for one day'. 焉 is the fused 於之 'to him'. 乎哉 doubles the final particles for a strong rhetorical question: 'does it come from others? surely not!' 克 kè is 'to overcome, to master'. Zhu Xi: 仁 is the whole virtue of the original mind; 克 is 'to conquer' (勝); 己 means the self's selfish desires (身之私欲); 復 is 'to go back' (反); 禮 is the measured pattern of Heaven's principle (天理之節文). The mind's whole virtue is nothing but Heaven's principle, yet it cannot help being spoiled by human desire, so one who practises humaneness must conquer selfish desire and go back to the rites. 歸 he glosses as 'to grant, to credit' (與): for one day do it, and everyone in the world will credit you with humaneness — the utmost of how swift and great its effect is; and 由己 shows that the hinge lies in me and is not hard. He quotes Master Cheng: wherever it is not the rites, there is selfish intention, and with selfish intention how can there be humaneness? And Xie Liangzuo (謝氏): overcome the self where one's nature is most lopsided and hardest to overcome. He Yan's commentary is plainer: Ma Rong takes 克己 as 'to restrain one's person' (約身); Kong Anguo's gloss on 復 is printed in this copy as 及 'to reach' — 'if one's person can reach the rites, that is humaneness'; Ma Rong on 一日: if in one day the world grants it, how much more over a lifetime; Kong Anguo: doing good lies with oneself, not with others.

sentences.t:
顔淵曰：「請問其目。」
子曰：「
非禮勿視，
非禮勿聽，
非禮勿言，
非禮勿動。」
顔淵曰：「
回雖不敏，
請事斯語矣。」

sentences.i: Yan Yuan said: “May I ask what it comes down to, point by point?” The Master said: “Whatever is out of keeping with the rites — do not look at it, do not listen to it, do not speak it, do not act on it.” Yan Yuan said: “I am slow, but with your leave I will make these words my work.”
sentences.n: 目 is 'the eye', and so the eyes or meshes of a net, the separate heads of a list — Zhu Xi: 目 are the particulars (條件). 非禮 'what is not ritual' is a fronted object, and 勿 is the prohibitive 'do not'. Hui calls himself by his personal name, as a pupil does before his master. 雖 'though'. 請 + verb 'allow me to'. 事 is 'to serve', here 'to make it one's business' (Zhu Xi: the 事 of 事事 'to see to things'). 語 yǔ 'words, a saying'. Zhu Xi: having heard the Master, Yan Yuan saw at once where Heaven's principle and human desire part, so he had no doubts to raise and asked straight for the items. 非禮 is one's own selfishness; 勿 is a word of prohibition — the hinge by which the mind takes command, overcomes selfishness and goes back to the rites. Yan Hui silently grasped the principle and knew he had the strength to win, so he took it on as his own charge without doubt. Master Cheng, quoted by Zhu Xi: these four are the workings of the body; they come from within and answer to what is without, and governing the outside is the way to nurture what is within. Zhu Xi prints the four admonitions (箴) Master Cheng wrote on seeing, hearing, speaking and moving, and adds: these exchanges are the most pressing words for handing on the method of the mind; only Yan Hui could be told them, yet every learner must strive at them. He Yan's Bao Xian: knowing there must be particular items, he asked for them; Zheng Xuan: these four are the items of 克己復禮; Wang Su: 'reverently making this saying my business' means he would surely carry it out.

sentences.t:
仲弓問仁。
子曰：「
出門如見大賓，
使民如承大祭。
己所不欲，
勿施於人。
在邦無怨，
在家無怨。」
仲弓曰：「
雍雖不敏，
請事斯語矣。」

sentences.l:
Zhonggong asked about humaneness.
The Master said: “Going out of your gate, be as if receiving a great guest;
employing the people, be as if carrying out a great sacrifice.
What you yourself do not want,
do not put upon others.
In the state, no resentment;
in the household, no resentment.”
Zhonggong said:
“Though I, Yong, am not quick,
let me make this saying my business.”
sentences.i: Zhonggong asked about humaneness. The Master said: “Once outside your door, carry yourself as though an honoured guest were before you; when you set the people to work, do it as though you were conducting a great sacrifice. Anything you would not wish for yourself, do not lay on anyone else. Then no one will bear you a grudge, in public life or at home.” Zhonggong said: “I am slow, but with your leave I will make these words my work.”
sentences.n: Two 如 'as if' lines, then a general rule, then its effect. 見 jiàn 'to see, to meet'; 大賓 'a great guest', as a lord receives another lord. 承 chéng is 'to receive, to carry out'; 祭 jì 'a sacrifice'. In 己所不欲, 己 'oneself' is the subject of the 所-phrase: 'what oneself does not want' — the whole is the fronted object of 施 'to lay on, impose'. Zhonggong is Ran Yong 冉雍 (6.1), who names himself Yong. His answer repeats Yan Yuan's, but for the name, as if the two exchanges were recorded as a pair. Zhu Xi: reverence to hold oneself, fellow-feeling (恕) to reach to others — then selfish intention has no room and the mind's virtue is whole; 'no resentment within or without' again speaks of the effect, so that he can test himself by it. Master Cheng, quoted by Zhu Xi: in speaking of humaneness the Master said only 'go out as if receiving a great guest, employ the people as if at a great sacrifice' — look at the bearing this implies; and asked about the times one is not going out or employing people, he answered that the reverence seen then shows the reverence that was there before. Zhu Xi's own comment: 克己復禮 is the way of Qian, holding to reverence and practising fellow-feeling the way of Kun (the strong and the yielding trigrams of the Changes), and here one sees the difference in height and depth between Yan Hui's learning and Ran Yong's; yet whoever truly works at reverence and fellow-feeling will find no self left to overcome. He Yan's Kong Anguo: in the way of humaneness nothing ranks above reverence; Bao Xian: 在邦 is serving as a feudal lord, 在家 as a minister or grandee (a 家 is a great house). The rule of 己所不欲 recurs in Book 15; compare Zigong's wish in 5.11.

sentences.t: 司馬牛問仁。

Sima (a surname; the title of a minister of war)

sentences.l: Sima Niu asked about humaneness.
sentences.i: Sima Niu asked about humaneness.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Sima Niu was a disciple of Confucius, personal name Li 犁, younger brother of Xiang Tui 向魋. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Niu was a man of Song, the disciple Sima Li 司馬犂; at 12.4 the same commentator calls the brother Huan Tui 桓魋 — the man of 7.22, whom Zhu Xi there identifies as Xiang Tui 向魋, minister of war in Song (桓魋宋司馬向魋也). 司馬 is the title 'master of horse', the minister of war (司 'in charge of', 馬 'horses'), here a family name. Three chapters in a row record Sima Niu, and each answer is fitted to the man.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
仁者，
其言也訒。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The humane man —
his speech is held back.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A humane man is slow to let his words out.”
sentences.n: 仁者 'the one who is humane'; 其言也訒 is topic + 也 + comment, 'his speech — held back'. 訒 rèn (Zhu Xi: 音刃) appears only here; Zhu Xi glosses it 忍 'holding in' and 難 'finding it hard': the humane man keeps his mind and does not let it run loose, so his words seem held in and do not come out easily — one facet of his virtue. The Master said this because Niu talked much and was hasty; if he were careful in this, the way to humaneness would lie right there. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 訒 is 'hard'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 其言也訒也, with a final 也.

sentences.t:
曰：「其言也訒，
斯謂之仁矣乎？」
子曰：「
為之難，
言之得無訒乎？」
sentences.l:
He said: “His speech held back —
is that then to be called humaneness?”
The Master said: “Doing it is hard;
speaking of it, can one help being held back?”
sentences.i: Niu said: “Slow to speak — is that all it takes to be called humane?” The Master said: “When the doing is so hard, how could a man be quick to talk of it?”
sentences.n: 斯 'this', at the head of a clause 'then, in that case'. 謂之仁 'call it humaneness'; 矣乎 together ask with some doubt 'is it already…?' — 'is that enough?' 為之 wéi 'doing it'; 難 nán 'hard'. 得無…乎 'can one avoid…?' is a rhetorical question expecting 'no'. Zhu Xi: Niu thought the way of humaneness was vast, not merely what the Master had said, so the Master told him: when the mind is kept, nothing is done carelessly, and when nothing is done carelessly, one's words naturally cannot come easily — not that one forcibly shuts them in. Yang Shi, quoted by Zhu Xi: from this and the second question in the next chapter one sees how lightly Niu spoke. Master Cheng, quoted by Zhu Xi: though it was said because of Niu's talkativeness, the sage's word goes just this far and is right. Zhu Xi adds: had the Master given a general account of humaneness, Niu's haste would never have let him think deeply and cure his fault; the sage's words differ in height and scope, but all touch the learner's own case. He Yan's Kong Anguo: doing humaneness is hard, so speaking of humaneness cannot but be hard too. Variants: He Yan's text reads 斯可謂之仁巳矣乎, adding 可 'can (be called)' and 巳 (= 已 'already'); Ruan Yuan's 1816 edition reads 斯謂之仁已乎, with 已 for 矣.

sentences.t:
司馬牛問君子。
子曰：「
君子不憂不懼。」

sentences.l:
Sima Niu asked about the gentleman.
The Master said: “The gentleman does not fret, does not fear.”
sentences.i: Sima Niu asked about the gentleman. The Master said: “The gentleman has no worries and no fears.”
sentences.n: 憂 is worry that sits in the heart, 懼 fear of what may come. Zhu Xi: Xiang Tui was stirring up rebellion and Niu was always anxious and afraid, so the Master told him this. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Niu's elder brother Huan Tui was about to rebel; Niu had come from Song to study and was always anxious and afraid, so the Master set his mind at ease.

sentences.t:
曰：「不憂不懼，
斯謂之君子矣乎？」
子曰：「
内省不疚，
夫何憂何懼？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He said: “Not fretting, not fearing —
is that then to be called a gentleman?”
The Master said: “Looking within, he finds nothing to sicken him;
then what is there to fret over, what to fear?”
sentences.i: Niu said: “No worries and no fears — is that all it takes to be called a gentleman?” The Master said: “If he looks into himself and finds nothing there to trouble him, what should he worry about, or fear?”
sentences.n: The question has the same frame as in 12.3 (斯謂之…矣乎). 内省 'look inward', 省 xǐng 'to examine'. 疚 jiù — Zhu Xi and He Yan's Bao Xian both gloss it 'sickness, a flaw' (病). 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶) opens the conclusion: 'now then'. 何憂何懼 'what to worry about, what to fear' — 何 before the verb asks for its object. Zhu Xi: Niu's second question is in the spirit of the last chapter, so the Master answered him again: because in his everyday conduct he has nothing to be ashamed of in his heart, he can look within and find no flaw, and so is naturally free of worry and fear — not something to be taken lightly as easy. He quotes Chao Yuezhi (晁氏): not worrying and not fearing come from virtue that is whole and without blemish, so that he is at ease wherever he goes — not that he really has worries and fears and forcibly drives them off. Bao Xian: looking within, he finds no fault or wrongdoing, so there is nothing to worry about or fear. Variants: He Yan's text reads 斯可謂君子巳乎 — 可 'can' added, no 之, and 巳 (= 已) for 矣; Ruan Yuan's 1816 edition reads 斯謂之君子已乎, with 已 for 矣.

sentences.t:
司馬牛憂曰：「
人皆有兄弟，
我獨亡。」

sentences.l:
Sima Niu was grieved and said: “Others all have brothers;
I alone have none.”
sentences.i: Sima Niu said sadly: “Everyone else has brothers. Only I have none.”
sentences.n: 亡 is read wú here, the same word as 無 'not to have' (as in 3.5). 獨 dú 'alone, only'. Zhu Xi: Niu had brothers, yet spoke so because he feared that they were making rebellion and would die for it. He Yan's commentary (the comment is headed 鄭之曰, apparently a slip for 鄭玄曰, Zheng Xuan): Niu's elder brother Huan Tui was doing evil and might die any day, and Niu felt he was as good as without brothers.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
商聞之矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zixia said: “I, Shang, have heard it said.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “Here is something I have heard.”
sentences.n: Zixia is Bu Shang 卜商 and calls himself by his personal name. 之 'it' points forward to the saying in the next unit; 矣 marks the hearing as done and settled. Zhu Xi: he had probably heard it from the Master. Zixia's speech runs on past two of Zhu Xi's comments; the quotation is closed here and the continuation units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
死生有命，
富貴在天。
sentences.l:
Death and life — there is a decree;
wealth and rank — they are with Heaven.
sentences.i: Whether we live or die is settled for us; whether we are rich or honoured is in Heaven's keeping.
sentences.n: A couplet in two matched halves: a pair of opposites as topic ('death and life', 'wealth and rank'), then a short comment. 有命 'there is a decree': 命 is what Heaven ordains. 在 'to lie with, to rest in'. Zhu Xi: the decree is received at the very beginning of life and cannot now be shifted; Heaven does things without anyone doing them, so they are not for me to make certain; one should simply accept them in compliance. The continuation of Zixia's speech is unquoted.

sentences.t:
君子敬而無失，
與人恭而有禮；
四海之内，
皆兄弟也。
君子何患乎無兄弟也？

the four seas — the whole world

sentences.l:
The gentleman is reverent and without lapse,
with others courteous and observing the rites;
inside the ring of the four seas,
everyone is his brother.
Why should the gentleman worry about having no brothers?
sentences.i: Let a gentleman be reverent and never slip, and meet others with courtesy and proper form, and every man the four seas enclose is a brother to him. Why should a gentleman fret that he has no brothers?
sentences.n: 敬而無失 'reverent and without lapse'; 與人 'with others, in dealing with others' (與 yǔ). 恭而有禮 'courteous and having the rites' — Zhu Xi: courteous, with measure and form (有節文). 四海 'the four seas' were thought to ring the inhabited land on every side, so 四海之内 is the whole world. 何患乎無兄弟 'why worry about having no brothers': 乎 here is the preposition 'about' (= 於). Still the unquoted continuation of Zixia's speech. Zhu Xi: once at peace with the decree, one should attend to what lies with oneself; if a man holds himself with reverence and without break and meets others with courtesy and due form, everyone in the world will love and respect him as a brother. Zixia wished to ease Niu's grief, and so said this as words wrung from necessity; readers should not let the wording spoil the meaning. Hu Yin (胡氏), quoted by Zhu Xi: Zixia's 'all are brothers' was said only to widen Sima Niu's thoughts — round in meaning but stiff in the words, a fault only a sage is free of; and Zixia, who knew this, still wept for his son until he lost his sight, blinded by love and dim to principle, so he could not live up to his own words. He Yan's Bao Xian: the gentleman keeps away from the bad and befriends the worthy, and the men of the nine regions can all be made kin to him by the rites. Variant: He Yan's text reads 四海之内皆爲兄弟也, 'all become (his) brothers'.

sentences.t:
子張問明。
子曰：「
浸潤之譖，
膚受之愬，
不行焉，
可謂明也已矣。
浸潤之譖，
膚受之愬，
不行焉，
可謂遠也已矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang asked about clear sight.
The Master said: “Slander that soaks in and seeps,
complaints felt on the skin —
if they get nowhere with him,
he may be called clear-sighted, and that is all.
Slander that soaks in and seeps,
complaints felt on the skin —
if they get nowhere with him,
he may be called far-sighted, and that is all.”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked what it is to see clearly. The Master said: “The slander that seeps in little by little, the grievance that stings like a blow to one's own skin — if neither works on a man, he can be called clear-sighted. If neither works on him, he can be called far-sighted.”
sentences.n: The same sentence twice, changing only its last word, for emphasis. 浸潤之譖 'soaking-seeping slander': 之 makes the first two words describe the noun. 譖 zèn is slander (Zhu Xi spells it 莊蔭反; we give the modern zèn); 愬 sù (蘇路反) is a complaint, the word later written 訴. 不行焉 'do not go (= get nowhere) with him': 行 xíng, 焉 = 於之. 也已矣 heaps up final particles: 'and that is all there is to it'. 遠 yuǎn 'far' (Zhu Xi marks no reading here). Zhu Xi: 浸潤 is like water steeping and soaking, sinking in by degrees and never all at once; 譖 is running down another's conduct; 膚受 is what the skin itself receives, harm that touches one's own person, as the Changes says 'the bed is split up to the skin'; 愬 is crying out one's own wrongs. Slander that seeps in gradually is believed deeply before the hearer notices; a grievance pressed urgently and close to oneself is acted on before the hearer has time to look into it. Both are hard to see through, and the man who does see through them has a clear mind not clouded by what is near. The Master must have said it to meet a fault of Zizhang's, and so repeated himself, to drive it home. Yang Shi, quoted by Zhu Xi: 遠 is clear sight at its utmost, and he cites the Documents, 'seeing far is clear sight'. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: the slanderer's words are like water soaking in, and by degrees bring about another man's ruin; Ma Rong: 膚受 is talk from the surface of the skin, not the inner truth; and on 遠, Ma Rong: not merely clear-sighted, but of virtue and conduct so high and far that no one can reach him.

sentences.t:
子貢問政。
子曰：「
足食，
足兵，
民信之矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong asked about government.
The Master said: “Enough food,
enough arms,
and the people trusting him.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked about government. The Master said: “See that there is food enough and arms enough, and the people will have faith in their ruler.”
sentences.n: Three short phrases. 足 zú is 'enough', put before its noun: 足食 'enough food'. 食 shí 'food'; 兵 bīng 'weapons, arms', and so the men who bear them. 民信之 'the people trust him', 之 being the ruler; 矣 marks the state reached. Zhu Xi reads it as a sequence: when the granaries are full and the military preparations in order, teaching can spread, and the people trust the ruler and do not break away. Variant: He Yan's text reads 使民信之矣 'and make the people trust them'.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
必不得已而去，
於斯三者何先？」
曰：「
去兵。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “If it must be, and there is no help for it, and one is given up —
of these three, which first?”
He said: “Give up arms.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “And if there were no help for it and one of the three had to go, which would go first?” “Arms.”
sentences.n: 不得已 'cannot manage to stop', so 'there is no help for it'; 必 'must' strengthens it. 於斯三者 'among these three things'; 何先 'which first?' 去 'to remove, to let go': Zhu Xi marks this verb 上聲 (qǔ), here and below (上聲下同); modern practice keeps qù, and so do we. Zhu Xi: if food is sufficient and good faith secure, the defence holds firm even without an army.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
必不得已而去，
於斯二者何先？」
曰：「
去食。
自古皆有死，
民無信不立。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “If it must be, and there is no help for it, and one is given up —
of these two, which first?”
He said: “Give up food.
Since of old all men have died;
the people without good faith do not stand.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “And if there were no help for it and one of the two remaining had to go, which would go first?” “Food. Men have always died, from the beginning; but take away good faith and a people cannot hold together at all.”
sentences.n: 自古 'from antiquity'; 皆有死 'all have death', everyone dies. 民無信不立 'the people without good faith do not stand': 立 is 'to stand, to be established'. Whose good faith? Zhu Xi takes it both ways: without food the people die, but death is something no one escapes; without good faith, though alive, they have nothing to stand by, and death would be easier. So the ruler would rather die than break faith with his people, and the people would rather die than break faith with him. He quotes Master Cheng: the Master's disciples asked well, pressing to the very bottom of a matter; only Zigong could have asked this, and only a sage could have answered. Zhu Xi's own comment: by ordinary feeling, food and arms must be enough before the ruler's good faith can win the people; but by the people's virtue, good faith is what men have in them from the start, and food and arms cannot come before it — so one who governs must lead his people in his own person and hold to it unto death, never dropping it for danger or haste. He Yan's Kong Anguo: death is the constant way of past and present, which all men share; in ruling a state one cannot lose good faith. Variants: He Yan's text has only 曰 'he said' (no 子貢) before Zigong's second question, and reads 民不信不立 'if the people do not trust, (the state) does not stand'.

sentences.t:
棘子成曰：「
君子質而已矣，
何以文為？」

morph.gloss: Ji Zicheng — a grandee of Wei
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ji Zicheng said: “The gentleman is plain stuff and that is all;
what use is pattern to him?”
sentences.i: Ji Zicheng said: “What makes a gentleman is his substance, and nothing more. What does he want with polish?”
sentences.n: 質 zhì 'plain stuff, substance' and 文 'pattern, polish' are the pair of 6.16. 而已矣 'and stop there': 'that is all'. 何以…為 is a fixed frame, 'what does one use… for?', with 為 wéi closing the question. Zhu Xi: Ji Zicheng was a grandee of Wei; he disliked the way pattern outran substance in the men of his day, and said this. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: by an old account Ji Zicheng was a grandee of Wei. Variant: He Yan's text writes the name 棘子城 and reads 何以文爲矣, with a final 矣.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
惜乎！
夫子之說，君子也；
駟不及舌。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zigong said: “What a pity. You mean it as a gentleman, sir — but once a word has left the tongue, not even four horses in harness can fetch it back.”
sentences.n: 惜乎 'what a pity!' 夫子 here is a courteous 'you, sir', addressed to Ji Zicheng, not the Master. 說 shuō 'what is said'. 駟 sì is a team of four horses, the fastest thing on the road. The punctuation follows Zhu Xi: what Ji Zicheng says is a gentleman's intent, but once words leave the tongue even a four-horse team cannot catch them, and Zigong regrets that he has misspoken. He Yan's Zheng Xuan simply repeats the words 惜乎夫子之說君子也 and adds: an overstatement once out, a team of four cannot overtake the tongue — which seems to take the line as one, 'a pity, sir, the way you speak of the gentleman!', the other common punctuation.

sentences.t:
文猶質也，
質猶文也。
虎豹之鞟猶犬羊之鞟。
sentences.i: Pattern counts for as much as substance, and substance for as much as pattern. Take the hair off a tiger's or a leopard's hide and you could not tell it from a dog's or a sheep's.
sentences.n: 猶 'is like, is as good as'. 鞟 kuò (Zhu Xi: 其郭反) is a hide with the hair taken off. The unquoted continuation of Zigong's answer. Zhu Xi: pattern and substance are equal and neither can do without the other; strip away all pattern and keep only substance, and there would be no telling the gentleman from the small man. But Ji Zicheng, correcting the fault of his age, went too far, and Zigong, correcting Ji Zicheng, lost the difference between root and branch, between weighty and light: both missed the mark. He Yan's Kong Anguo: a hide with the hair removed is 鞹; tigers and leopards differ from dogs and sheep only by the pattern of their fur, and if pattern and substance were made the same, how would one tell them apart? Variant: He Yan's text ends 犬羊之鞹也, with a final 也.

sentences.t:
哀公問於有若曰：「
年饑，
用不足，
如之何？」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Duke Ai asked You Ruo: “The harvest has failed,
there is not enough for our needs —
what is to be done?”
sentences.i: Duke Ai put a question to You Ruo: “It has been a year of dearth, and the revenue will not cover what we spend. What is to be done?”
sentences.n: Duke Ai is the ruler of Lu (2.19); You Ruo is the disciple the book elsewhere calls Master You (有子, 1.2). Zhu Xi: he is called by his full name here because these are words between ruler and minister. 年饑 'the year is a famine': 饑 jī is a failure of the grain. 用 is 'spending' — Zhu Xi: the state's outlay; the duke's thought was to raise the levy to cover it. 如之何 'what to do about it?'

sentences.t:
有若對曰：「
盍徹乎？」
sentences.l: You Ruo replied: “Why not the tithe?”
sentences.i: You Ruo replied: “Why not go back to taking a tenth?”
sentences.n: 對 is the word for answering a superior. 盍 is the fused 何不 'why not?' 徹 chè is the name of the Zhou tax of one part in ten. Zhu Xi: 徹 means 'to go through, to even out' (通也，均也). Under the Zhou system each man received a hundred mu of land and worked it together with those who shared his ditch and well; the harvest was reckoned by the mu and divided, the people keeping roughly nine parts and the duke taking one — hence the name. Lu, from Duke Xuan's time on, also taxed each mu, taking another tenth, so the levy had become two parts in ten; You Ruo asks the duke simply to keep to the tithe, wanting him to spend less and deal generously with the people. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 盍 is 'why not'; under the Zhou law, a tax of one in ten was called 徹, and 徹 means 'common', the law common to the whole realm.

sentences.t:
曰：「
二，
吾猶不足，
如之何其徹也？」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.i: The duke said: “I take two tenths and it is still not enough. How could I manage on one?”
sentences.n: 二 'two' is short for two parts in ten. 猶 'still'. 如之何其徹也 'what about it, my tithing?' — that is, 'how could I tithe?'; 其 before the verb softens it into a musing question. Zhu Xi: 二 is the two-in-ten just mentioned; the duke thought You Ruo had not caught his drift, and said this to show that he meant to raise the levy. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 二 means a tax of two in ten.

sentences.t:
對曰：「
百姓足，
君孰與不足？
百姓不足，
君孰與足？」

morph.gloss: surname, clan name (同姓 'the same surname', Zhu Xi: 禮不娶同姓, 'the rites do not take a wife of one's own surname')

sentences.l:
He replied: “The people having enough —
with whom would the lord not have enough?
The people not having enough —
with whom would the lord have enough?”
sentences.i: He replied: “When the people have enough, how could their lord be the one who goes short? When the people go short, how could their lord be the one who has enough?”
sentences.n: 百姓 'the hundred clans' is the whole people. 孰與 'with whom': 孰 is 'who' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 孰，誰也) and 與 yǔ 'with', the question word put before its preposition. The two halves mirror each other: 'who would the lord share want with?' Zhu Xi: when the people are rich, the lord will not be poor alone; when the people are poor, the lord cannot be rich alone. You Ruo is pressing the thought that lord and people are one body, to stop the duke's heavy exactions — something every man set over others should ponder. He quotes Yang Shi: humane government begins with the field boundaries; once they are true, the well-fields are even and salaries fair, and the needs of army and state are measured from them, so with the tithe alone a hundred measures follow. One in ten is the just mean for the world; to take more is the way of the tyrant Jie, to take less that of the barbarian Mo; later ages sought the branch and not the root, and so above and below were both in want.

sentences.t:
子張問崇徳辨惑。
子曰：「
主忠信，
徙義，
崇徳也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang asked about exalting virtue and sorting out delusion.
The Master said: “Take as chief wholeheartedness and good faith,
move toward what is right:
that is exalting virtue.”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked how to raise up virtue and see through delusion. The Master said: “Hold to wholeheartedness and good faith above all, and shift your ground toward what is right: that is how virtue is raised up.”
sentences.n: 崇 chóng 'to heighten, to exalt'; 辨 biàn 'to tell apart, to sort out'; 惑 'delusion, being led astray'. 主忠信 is the maxim of 1.8 and 9.24, and is given the same English. 徙 'to move, to shift (one's ground)'. The answer to the first half of the question ends here, closed by 也; the second half comes in the next unit. Zhu Xi: hold to wholeheartedness and good faith, and the root is set; move toward what is right, and one is renewed day by day. He Yan's Bao Xian: 辨 is 'to distinguish'; 徙義 is, on seeing what is right, to let one's mind shift over and follow it. Fan Chi asks about the same pair, with a third item, in 12.21.

sentences.t:
愛之欲其生，
惡之欲其死。
既欲其生，
又欲其死：
是惑也。
sentences.l:
Loving someone, you want him to live;
hating him, you want him to die.
Already wanting him to live,
you also want him to die:
this is delusion.
sentences.i: We love a man and wish him life; we hate him and wish him death. To wish him life and then wish him death as well — that is delusion.
sentences.n: The unquoted continuation of the Master's answer. 惡 wù 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), against 愛 'to love'. 欲其生 'want him to live': 其 is the subject of the little clause after 欲. 既…又… 'already…, and then also…'. 是 'this' sums up what precedes. Zhu Xi: love and hate are ordinary human feelings, but a man's life and death are fated and cannot be had by wanting; to want a man alive or dead because one loves or hates him is delusion, and to want both for the same man is delusion at its worst. He Yan's Bao Xian: love and hate should hold steady; to want him alive one moment and dead the next is a deluded mind. Variant: He Yan's text reads 愛之欲其生也，惡之欲其死也, with 也 after each half, and ends 是惑 without the final 也.

sentences.t:
誠不以富，
亦祗以異。
sentences.l:
Truly it does not lead to riches;
it serves only to mark one out as strange.
sentences.i: In truth it brings no riches; all it brings is the name of being odd.
sentences.n: Two lines of an Ode, still unquoted (as 9.30), since the speech runs on. 誠 'truly'. 以 'by it, so as to'. 祗 is read zhǐ 'only, just': the edition (and Ruan's) writes 祗, properly zhī 'reverent', for 祇 'only' — He Yan's Zheng Xuan glosses it 適 'just, merely'. Zhu Xi: these are words from the Lesser Odes, the poem 我行其野 'I go through the open country'. By the old explanation the Master quoted them to show that wanting a man alive or dead cannot make him so — like the Ode's 'truly not enough to bring wealth, only enough to earn the name of strange'. But he quotes Master Cheng: this is a displaced slip and belongs in Book 16, after 齊景公有馬千駟 'Duke Jing of Qi had a thousand teams of four'; it strayed here because the passage that follows also begins with Duke Jing of Qi. Zheng Xuan: this is from the Lesser Odes; such conduct truly cannot bring wealth and only makes one strange — the Master takes the Ode's word 'strange' to censure it.

sentences.t: 齊景公問政於孔子。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Duke Jing of Qi asked Kongzi about government.
sentences.i: Duke Jing of Qi asked Kongzi about government.
sentences.n: Qi was the large state east and north of Lu. Zhu Xi: Duke Jing of Qi was named Chujiu 杵臼; in the last years of Duke Zhao of Lu, Confucius went to Qi. 問政於孔子 'asked about government of Confucius': 於 marks the person asked. The book calls him 孔子 'Master Kong' when he deals with a ruler.

sentences.t:
孔子對曰：「
君君，
臣臣，
父父，
子子。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi replied: “The lord acting the lord,
the minister acting the minister,
the father acting the father,
the son acting the son.”
sentences.i: Kongzi replied: “It is for the lord to behave as a lord should, the minister as a minister should, the father as a father should, and the son as a son should.”
sentences.n: Eight characters, four pairs: in each the first word is the noun and the second the same word used as a verb, 'to be truly (that)', 'to do what the name requires'. Zhu Xi: this is the great warp of the human Way and the root of all government. At the time Duke Jing had let government slip from his hands, the grandee Chen clan was winning the state with lavish gifts, and the duke kept many favourites in his inner palace and had named no heir; between lord and minister, father and son, the Way was lost on every side, and so the Master told him this. He Yan's Kong Anguo: at that time Chen Huan (so the comment names him) held Qi in his grip, the lord was no lord and the minister no minister, hence the answer.

sentences.t:
公曰：「
善哉！
信如君不君，
臣不臣，
父不父，
子不子，
雖有粟，
吾得而食諸？」
sentences.l:
The duke said: “Good indeed!
Truly, if the lord is not lord,
the minister not minister,
the father not father,
the son not son,
though there be grain,
would I get to eat it?”
sentences.i: The duke said: “Well spoken! Truly, if the lord is no lord and the minister no minister, if the father is no father and the son no son, then though there were grain in store, could I count on eating any of it?”
sentences.n: 善哉 'good — how!': the predicate put first for exclamation. 信如 'if truly'. 君不君 'the lord does not act the lord', the same noun-as-verb as before, negated. 諸 here is the fused 之乎 'it?' (as 7.34 有諸): 得而食諸 'get to eat it?' The duke hears the answer as a warning for his own skin. Zhu Xi: Duke Jing approved the Master's words but could not use them; in the end, by leaving the succession unsettled, he opened the way to the Chen clan's murder of the ruler and seizure of the state. Yang Shi, quoted by Zhu Xi: lord, minister, father and son each have the way that makes them so; Duke Jing knew to approve the words but did not seek back for the reason — pleased but not unravelling it (as 9.23), which is why Qi ended in disorder. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he speaks of danger to come; the Chen clan did in the end destroy Qi. Variant: He Yan's text reads 吾豈得而食諸 'how could I get to eat it?', adding 豈 'how'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
片言可以折獄者，
其由也與？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who with half a word can decide a lawsuit —
surely it is Yóu, is it not?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If there is anyone who can settle a case on half a word, it must be Yóu.”
sentences.n: 片言 is 'half a word' on Zhu Xi's reading (片言，半言), and 折 zhé (Zhu Xi: 之舌反) is 'to break', hence 'to decide' (折，斷也); 獄 is a lawsuit or criminal case. 可以 'can (by means of it)'; 者 closes the phrase into 'the one who…'. 其…也與 is the tentative 'surely it is…, is it not?', with 與 the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 由 is Zilu's personal name, written Yóu as in Book 11. Zhu Xi: Zilu was wholehearted and of good faith, clear and decisive, so that when he spoke men believed him and accepted it without waiting for him to finish. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads 片 as 偏 'one side': hearing a suit needs the statements of both parties to settle right and wrong; to decide a case trusting one side's words — only Zilu could do that.

sentences.t: 子路無宿諾。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zilu had no promise kept overnight.
sentences.i: Zilu never let a promise wait till the next day.
sentences.n: 宿 sù is 'to stay the night', hence 'to keep over, hold back'; 諾 is the word of assent, 'yes', and so a promise. Zhu Xi: 宿 is 留 'to keep', as in 宿怨 'a grudge one keeps'; Zilu was eager to make good his word and never let a promise lie. He prints the line in one chapter with the Master's saying before it: the recorders, he says, set it down there to show that Zilu won men's trust because he had trained himself to it all along. He quotes Yin Tun's example: a man of the small state of Little Zhu (小邾射) fled to Lu with the town of 句繹 and said, 'If Ji Lu makes the compact with me, I need no oath' — a state of a thousand chariots would not trust its own oath, yet trusted one word of Zilu's; one word could settle a case because the good faith came before the words, and he kept no promise waiting so as to keep that faith whole. He Yan's commentary reads 宿 another way, as 'beforehand' (宿猶豫也): Zilu held so firmly to his word that, fearing things might change when the time came, he made no promises in advance.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
聽訟，
吾猶人也。
必也使無訟乎！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Hearing lawsuits,
I am like others.
If it must be anything, it would be making there be no lawsuits!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “At hearing cases I do as anyone does. What I would want is that there be no cases to hear.”
sentences.n: 聽訟 'to listen to suits', that is, to try cases. 猶人 'like others'. 必也…乎 is the shape of 3.7 (必也射乎): 'if it must be something, it would be…'. 使無訟 'to cause there to be no suits': 使 'to make (it so that)'. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: hearing suits deals with the branches and dams the flow; set the root right and clear the source, and there will be no suits. And Yang Shi: Zilu could decide a case with half a word, but did not know how to govern a state by the rites and deference, and so could not bring the people to have no suits; the recorders set this saying after the last to show that the sage did not count hearing suits hard, but valued making the people have none. In He Yan, Bao Xian (苞氏): 'I am the same as others'; Wang Su: to have no suits is to transform the people beforehand.

sentences.t:
子張問政。
子曰：「
居之無倦，
行之以忠。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zizhang asked about governing. The Master said: “Keep it in your mind and never tire of it; and in whatever you do in it, be wholehearted.”
sentences.n: Two matching clauses, verb + 之 'it' + how: 居之無倦 'dwell on it without wearying', 行之以忠 'carry it out with wholeheartedness'. 居 'to dwell, abide in'; 倦 'to weary'; 行 xíng 'to carry out'. Zhu Xi: 居 means keeping it in the heart — without wearying, beginning and end are one; 行 means putting it forth in affairs — with wholeheartedness, outside and inside are one. He quotes Master Cheng: Zizhang was short of humaneness; without a sincere heart that loves the people one is bound to tire and not give one's whole mind, so the Master told him this. He Yan's Wang Su: in the way of governing, hold it in one's own person without slackening, and carry it to the people always with wholeheartedness and good faith.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
博學於文，
約之以禮，
亦可以弗畔矣夫！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Learning broadly in letters
and drawing it in by the rites,
one can also keep from turning away!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Learn widely in the written tradition and gather it in by the rites, and you too can keep from turning your back on the Way.”
sentences.n: The saying of 6.25 again, and the English is kept; Zhu Xi notes only 重出 'it appears twice'. There it has 君子 'the gentleman' as subject; Zhu Xi's text here has none, and the English supplies 'one'. 約 yuē 'to draw in, bring to the essential' (Zhu Xi at 6.25: 要也); 弗 fú 'not'; 畔 pàn 'to turn one's back on' (= 叛); 夫 fú closes the exclamation. He Yan glosses here, in his own words, 弗畔 as 'not going against the Way'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子曰君子博學於文, with 君子 as at 6.25.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子成人之美，
不成人之惡。
小人反是。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman helps the good in other people to its fulfilment and gives no help to the bad. With the small man it is the other way round.”
sentences.n: 成 'to complete, bring about'; 美 'fine, beautiful' — here what is good in a man; 惡 è 'bad' (not wù 'to hate'). 人之美 / 人之惡: 之 is the genitive 'others' good / others' bad'. 反是 'reverses this', 是 'this' pointing back to the whole. Zhu Xi: 成 is to draw a man on, support him, encourage and reward him, so that his undertaking comes to completion; the gentleman and the small man differ in what they hold to, generous or mean, and in what they like, good or bad, and so the way they use their hearts differs like this.

sentences.t:
季康子問政於孔子。
孔子對曰：「
政者，正也。
子帥以正，
孰敢不正？」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
Kang, posthumous name of Ji Kangzi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ji Kangzi asked Kongzi about government.
Kongzi answered, saying: “Government is setting right.
You, sir, lead by being right —
who would dare not be right?”
sentences.i: Ji Kangzi asked Kongzi about governing. Kongzi answered: “To govern is to put straight. Go before them straight yourself, sir, and who will dare to be crooked?”
sentences.n: 政 zhèng 'government' is written with 正 zhèng 'straight, right' and sounds the same: the answer is a definition by pun, in the frame X者Y也 'X is Y'. 子 is 'you, sir', polite address to a grandee; 帥 shuài 'to lead'; 孰敢 'who would dare'. Ji Kangzi is the head of the Ji house (2.20). Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: no one who was not upright himself has ever set others upright. And Hu Yin: from the middle of its history the government of Lu had been in the grandees' hands, and their household retainers copied them, seizing towns and rising in revolt — unrightness at its worst; so Kongzi told him this, hoping Kangzi would master himself by uprightness and undo the old ways of the three houses — sadly Kangzi was sunk in desire for gain and could not. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: Ji Kangzi was the senior minister of Lu, the leader (帥) of all its ministers. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子帥而正 'if you lead and are right'.

sentences.t:
季康子患盜，
問於孔子。
孔子對曰：「
苟子之不欲，
雖賞之，不竊。」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
Kang, posthumous name of Ji Kangzi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ji Kangzi was troubled by thieves
and asked Kongzi about it.
Kongzi answered, saying: “If you yourself, sir, were free of wanting,
though you paid them for it, they would not steal.”
sentences.i: Ji Kangzi was worried about thieving and asked Kongzi what to do. Kongzi answered: “Were you, sir, without greed yourself, you could offer the people a reward for stealing and they still would not.”
sentences.n: 盜 dào 'a thief; to rob'; 竊 qiè 'to steal'. 苟 'if'. 子之不欲 'your not desiring': 之 between subject and verb turns the clause into a noun, here the condition. 欲 is desire, appetite (Kong Anguo in He Yan: 情慾). 雖 'even if'; 賞之 'reward them' — Zhu Xi: even if you rewarded the people to make thieves of them, they would know shame and not steal. He quotes Hu Yin: the Ji had stolen the handle of power and Kangzi had snatched the place of the rightful heir (the comment adds that the affair of the heir is told in the commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals, 春秋傳); that the people turned thief was only to be expected — why not go back to the root? Kongzi opened the matter with 'not desiring', and the point runs deep. Kong Anguo: the people are changed by those above; they follow not what they are ordered but what their superior likes. Variant: He Yan's text reads 苟子不欲, without 之 — the same sense.

sentences.t:
季康子問政於孔子曰：「
如殺無道，
以就有道，
何如？」
孔子對曰：「
子為政，
焉用殺？
子欲善，
而民善矣。
君子之徳風，
小人之徳草。
草上之風，
必偃。」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
Kang, posthumous name of Ji Kangzi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ji Kangzi asked Kongzi about government, saying: “If I killed those without the Way
so as to bring on those with the Way —
how would that be?”
Kongzi answered, saying: “You, sir, conduct the government:
what use have you for killing?
You want the good,
and the people are good.
The gentleman's virtue — wind;
the small man's virtue — grass.
The grass, lay the wind on it:
it must lie flat.”
sentences.i: Ji Kangzi asked Kongzi about governing: “What if I put to death those who are without the Way, to help on those who have it?” Kongzi answered: “You are the one who governs, sir — why reach for killing? Want the good, and the people will turn good. In the gentleman, virtue is the wind; in the small man, it is the grass. Lay wind across grass, and it is bound to lie down.”
sentences.n: 如 'if'. 殺 is shā 'to kill' (in 10.6 the same graph was shài). 無道 / 有道 are 'those without / those with the Way'; 就 'to go toward', hence 'to bring about' (Kong Anguo in He Yan: 就，成也 — he wanted to kill many to put a stop to wickedness). 焉 yān 'what? how?' (Zhu Xi: 於䖍反): 焉用殺 'what use (is) killing'. 子欲善而民善矣: 而 links cause and effect, 'want the good, and so the people are good'. Here 君子 and 小人 are those above and those below, as the figure shows. 草上之風: Zhu Xi says another text writes 上 as 尚, 'to add, to lay on' (加也): 'the grass — lay the wind on it'; 偃 is 'to fall flat' (仆也). Zhu Xi: the one who governs is what the people watch and copy — why kill? Want the good and the people will be good. He quotes Yin Tun: 'kill' — how can that be the talk of one set over others? Teach by one's own person and men follow; teach by words and they argue; how much more if one teaches by killing! Kong Anguo: he wanted Kangzi to set himself right first; grass with the wind laid on it all goes down, as the people are changed by those above. Variants in He Yan's text: 子爲改焉用殺, with 改 'to change' where Zhu Xi has 政 — it gives no good sense and is probably a slip of the copyist or cutter for the similar 政, though this cannot be proved from here; 君子之徳風也，小人之徳草也, each with a closing 也; and 草尚之風, the 尚 that Zhu Xi mentions.

sentences.t:
子張問：「
士何如斯可謂之達矣？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l: Zizhang asked: “An officer — being how, can he then be called one who makes his way?”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked what it takes for an officer to be called a man who has made his way.
sentences.n: 士 shì 'an officer, a man of service' (4.9). 何如斯可謂之X矣 'being how, then can (he) be called X?': 何如 'how, of what kind', 斯 'then', 謂之 'call him'. 達 dá is 'to get through, to reach' — of a man, to make his way, to go everywhere unhindered. Zhu Xi: 達 is when one's virtue is trusted by others and nothing one does fails to get through. Variant: He Yan's text ends 斯可謂之達也, with 也 for 矣.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
何哉，
爾所謂達者？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “What is it,
this that you call making one's way?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “And what do you mean by making one's way?”
sentences.n: 何哉 'what is it?' comes first, then the subject, 爾所謂達者 'the thing you call 達': 所 + verb is 'what is (verbed)', and 者 closes the phrase. Zhu Xi: Zizhang worked at the outward; the Master already knew what lay behind the question, and so turned it back on him, to bring out the illness before prescribing for it. Variant: He Yan's text reads 爾所謂達者矣.

sentences.t:
子張對曰：「
在邦必聞，
在家必聞。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang answered, saying: “In a state, he is sure to be heard of;
in a house, he is sure to be heard of.”
sentences.i: Zizhang answered: “Whether he serves a state or a noble house, his name is known.”
sentences.n: 邦 is a state, under its lord; 家 is the house of a grandee (大夫). 聞 'to hear' is here 'to be heard of', a passive with no mark: the verb alone serves. Zhu Xi: it means that his name and repute are widely heard. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: wherever the officer is, he has a name.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
是聞也，
非達也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “This is being heard of;
it is not making one's way.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “That is having a name. It is not making one's way.”
sentences.n: 是…也，非…也 'this is X, it is not Y'. Zhu Xi: being heard of and making one's way look alike and are not the same — this is where the true and the false part, and the learner must look closely; so the Master first marks the difference plainly, and the lines that follow set each out at length. The Master's speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next two units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
夫達也者，
質直而好義，
察言而觀色，
慮以下人；
在邦必達，
在家必達。
sentences.i: Making one's way is this: to be plain and straight and to love what is right, to weigh what people say and watch their faces, and to take care to place oneself beneath them. Such a man makes his way in a state, and makes his way in a great house.
sentences.n: 夫 fú opens a new topic, 'now' (Zhu Xi: 音扶); 也者 after 達 marks it for definition, 'as for making one's way…'. 質 'plain stuff, substance' (as against 文); 好 hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 下 is a verb, 'to put below': 下人 'to place oneself under others' (Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, the verbal reading, which modern Mandarin simply reads xià). 慮以 'to take thought how to'. Zhu Xi: within, he holds to wholeheartedness and good faith, and what he does fits what is right; he is careful in dealing with others and humbly keeps himself low — all matters of working on oneself within, not of seeking to be known; yet when virtue is cultivated in oneself and others trust it, nothing one does meets a block. He Yan's Ma Rong: such a man always means to be modest and give way; examining words and seeing faces, he knows what others want, and his thought is always to put himself below them; and on 'sure to make his way' he quotes 'modesty, honoured, shines; lowly, it cannot be overstepped' (謙尊而光，卑而不可踰). Unquoted: the Master's speech continues from the unit before. Variant: He Yan's text reads 夫達者, without 也.

sentences.t:
夫聞也者，
色取仁而行違，
居之不疑；
在邦必聞，
在家必聞。
sentences.l:
Now being heard of:
in his look he takes up humaneness, but his conduct goes against it,
and he settles in it without a doubt —
in a state he is sure to be heard of,
in a house he is sure to be heard of.
sentences.i: Being heard of is this: to wear the look of humaneness while acting against it, and to rest easy in the part without a qualm. Such a man is talked of in a state, and talked of in a great house.
sentences.n: Built on the frame of the unit before. 色取仁 'in the face, takes up humaneness': 色 'look, countenance' is used adverbially. 行 is 'conduct' — Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, xìng, the noun; modern practice reads xíng, as at 11.2. 居之不疑 'dwells in it and has no doubt'. Zhu Xi: he puts on a good face to lay hold of humaneness while in fact his deeds turn their back on it, and he thinks himself right and has no scruple; this is a man who does not work at the real but only seeks a name, so his empty repute may run high while his real virtue is sick. He quotes Master Cheng: the learner must work at the real and keep away from fame; once he means to court a name the great root is already lost — what more is there to learn? And Yin Tun: Zizhang's fault was that he did not work at the real, so everything Kongzi told him was solid and real, filling him within and showing without. He Yan's Ma Rong: this speaks of the glib man, who borrows the look of the humane but acts against it, rests in his falseness and does not doubt himself; such men have many partisans — hence 'sure to be heard of'. Unquoted: the speech continues. Variant: He Yan's text reads 夫聞者, without 也.

sentences.t:
樊遲從遊於舞雩之下，
曰：「敢問
崇徳、脩慝、辨惑。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l:
Fan Chi, following along, strolled below the rain-dance terrace.
He said: “May I venture to ask about
exalting virtue, working away hidden evil, and sorting out delusion?”
sentences.i: Fan Chi was out walking with the Master below the rain-dance terrace. He said: “May I ask how one raises one's virtue higher, clears out the evil hidden in oneself, and sees through one's own delusions?”
sentences.n: 從遊 'to follow and stroll', to go about with the Master; 從 cóng. 舞雩 is the rain-dance terrace of 11.25; He Yan's Bao Xian: the place of the rain dance had an altar, a levelled ground and trees, so one could stroll beneath them. 敢問 'I venture to ask', a polite formula. 崇 'to raise high, to honour'; 辨 'to tell apart, sort out'; 惑 'delusion, being led astray'. 慝 tè (Zhu Xi: 吐得反) — Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: the graph has 心 'heart' and 匿 'hidden', evil hidden in the heart; 脩 (the edition's form of 修) is to work on it and clear it away. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 慝 is 惡 'evil', 脩 is 治 'to work on' — to work on evil and make it good. Zizhang asked about 崇徳 and 辨惑 at 12.10.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
善哉問！」
sentences.l: The Master said: “How good, the question!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A fine question!”
sentences.n: 善哉問 puts the predicate first for an exclamation, 'good — how! — the question', as 孝哉閔子騫 (11.4). Zhu Xi: he praised it because it bore closely on doing for oneself (為己). The answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
先事後得，
非崇徳與？
攻其惡，無攻人之惡，
非脩慝與？
一朝之忿，
忘其身，以及其親，
非惑與？
sentences.l:
Put the work first and the gain last —
is that not exalting virtue?
Attack your own evil, do not attack the evil of others —
is that not working away hidden evil?
One morning's anger,
forgetting your own person and reaching even to your parents —
is that not delusion?
sentences.i: Do the work first and think of the reward afterwards: is that not how virtue is raised? Go after the wrong in yourself and leave alone the wrong in others: is that not how hidden evil is cleared out? To flare up for one morning, forget your own safety and drag your parents into it: is that not delusion?
sentences.n: Three answers in one frame, each closed by 非…與 'is it not…?', 與 yú the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 先事後得: 先 and 後 are verbs, 'put first', 'put last'. 攻 'to attack, to work at'; 其惡 'one's own evil', 惡 è; 無 'do not'. 一朝之忿 'one morning's anger', 朝 zhāo — a passing fit of temper. 以及其親 'and so reach to one's parents' (親 'kin, parents'). Zhu Xi: 先事後得 is like 先難後獲 of 6.20; do what should be done without reckoning the result, and virtue piles up day by day without one's knowing it; give oneself wholly to working on oneself and not blaming others, and one's own evil has nowhere to hide; know that a morning's anger is very small and disaster reaching one's parents very great, and one can sort out the delusion and curb the anger. Fan Chi was coarse and close to profit, he says, so he was told these three things, each to remedy a failing. He quotes Fan Zuyu: putting the work first and the gain after is to rank what is right above profit; nothing moves a man as easily as anger; the worst delusions always start from something small — sort them out early and they will not grow; so curbing anger is the way to sort out delusion. He Yan's Kong Anguo: first toil at the work, and afterwards get the reward. Unquoted: the Master's answer continues from the unit before. Variant: He Yan's text reads 毋攻人之惡, with the prohibitive 毋 for 無 — the same sense.

sentences.t:
樊遲問仁。
子曰：「愛人。」
問知。
子曰：「知人。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l:
Fan Chi asked about humaneness.
The Master said: “Loving others.”
He asked about wisdom.
The Master said: “Knowing others.”
sentences.i: Fan Chi asked what humaneness is. The Master said: “To love people.” He asked what wisdom is. The Master said: “To know people.”
sentences.n: The same graph twice in two readings: 問知 is zhì 'wisdom' (Zhu Xi: the first 知 is 去聲, and so below), 知人 is zhī 'to know (others)'. 人 is 'others, people', as against oneself. Zhu Xi: loving others is humaneness put to work; knowing others is the business of wisdom.

sentences.t: 樊遲未達。

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l: Fan Chi did not yet get through it.
sentences.i: Fan Chi did not understand.
sentences.n: 未達 'had not yet got through' — the 達 of 12.20, here of understanding. Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Zeng (曾氏): Chi's thought was that love wants to reach everyone while knowing involves choosing, so he suspected the two pulled against each other.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
舉直錯諸枉，
能使枉者直。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Raise the straight, set aside the many crooked,
and it can make the crooked straight.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Raise up the upright and set aside all the crooked, and you can make the crooked upright.”
sentences.n: The first half is 2.19 word for word (there the people submit), and the English is kept. 錯 cuò 'to set aside' (Zhu Xi at 2.19: 捨置); 諸 he glossed there as 衆 'the many', and here he simply writes 舉直錯枉 'raising the straight and setting aside the crooked'; others take 諸 as the fused 之於, 'set them over the crooked'. 能使…直 'can make… straight'; 枉者 'the crooked ones'. Zhu Xi: raising the straight and setting aside the crooked is wisdom; making the crooked straight is humaneness — so the two are not only not at odds, they work for each other. He Yan's Bao Xian: raise upright men and employ them, set aside and discard the crooked, and all are changed and become straight.

sentences.t:
樊遲退，
見子夏曰：「
鄉也吾見於夫子而問知，
子曰『舉直錯諸枉，能使枉者直』，
何謂也？」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Fan Chi withdrew,
saw Zixia and said: “A while ago I presented myself to the Master and asked about wisdom;
the Master said, ‘Raise the straight, set aside the many crooked, and it can make the crooked straight.’
What does that mean?”
sentences.i: Fan Chi withdrew and went to see Zixia. “Just now,” he said, “I was with the Master and asked about wisdom, and he said: ‘Raise up the upright and set aside all the crooked, and you can make the crooked upright.’ What did he mean?”
sentences.n: 鄉 is xiàng, the word later written 嚮, 'a while ago' (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 也 after it marks a pause. 見 is read two ways here: 見子夏 jiàn 'saw Zixia'; 見於夫子 xiàn 'presented myself to the Master' (Zhu Xi: 賢遍反), as at 3.24. 知 zhì 'wisdom'. 何謂也 'what does it mean?': the question word 何 comes before its verb 謂. Zhu Xi: Chi took the Master's words to be only about the wise man's business, and still had not grasped how it could make the crooked straight.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
富哉言乎！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zixia said: “How rich, the words!”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “There is a great deal in those words!”
sentences.n: Predicate first again, with 哉 'how!'; 乎 here closes the exclamation. Zhu Xi: he marvels at how wide its reach is — it speaks not only of wisdom. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 富 is 盛 'abundant'. Zixia's speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 富哉是言乎 'how rich are these words!'.

sentences.t:
舜有天下，
選於衆，舉臯陶，
不仁者遠矣。
湯有天下，
選於衆，舉伊尹，
不仁者遠矣。
sentences.l:
Shun held the world:
he chose from among the many and raised up Gao Yao,
and those without humaneness were far off.
Tang held the world:
he chose from among the many and raised up Yi Yin,
and those without humaneness were far off.
sentences.i: When Shun had the world, he picked out Gao Yao from among all the people and raised him up, and men without humaneness were nowhere to be found. When Tang had the world, he picked out Yi Yin from among all the people and raised him up, and men without humaneness were nowhere to be found.
sentences.n: Zixia's answer, continuing unquoted. Shun is the sage king who followed Yao. Gao Yao 臯陶 (陶 read yáo, Zhu Xi: 音遙) is the man Shun raised up; the comments here say no more of him, and tradition makes him Shun's minister in charge of punishments. Tang 湯 is in tradition the founder of the Shang; Yi Yin 伊尹 was his chief minister (Zhu Xi: 湯之相). 選 'to choose' — Zhu Xi marks it 息戀反 (xuàn), a reading modern practice does not keep; we give xuǎn. 遠 is yuǎn 'far' — Zhu Xi marks it 如字, its plain reading, not the verb yuàn 'to keep away'. 有天下 'to have the world', to reign. Zhu Xi: 'the inhumane were far off' means that everyone was changed and became humane, and no inhumane man was to be seen, as though they had gone far away — that is 'making the crooked straight'; Zixia saw that the Master's words held humaneness and wisdom together. He quotes Master Cheng: the sage's words change with the man; though some seem shallow and near, there is nothing they do not hold, as this chapter shows — unlike others' words, which speaking of the near leave out the far, and speaking of the far do not know the near. And Yin Tun: the learners of that day worked at the real — having asked their teacher, they sorted it out with a friend. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Shun and Tang, having the world, chose from the many and raised Gao Yao and Yi Yin; then the inhumane were far off and the humane arrived. Variant: He Yan's text reads 湯有天下選衆, without 於 — the same sense.

sentences.t:
子貢問友。
子曰：「忠告而善道之，
不可則止，
毋自辱焉。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zigong asked how to deal with a friend. The Master said: “Advise him with your whole heart and guide him with well-chosen words. If that does not serve, stop there, and do not bring humiliation on yourself.”
sentences.n: 忠告 'to advise wholeheartedly': 忠 works as an adverb. 告 'to tell, to advise' — Zhu Xi reads it 工毒反 (gù, an old reading for admonishing); modern practice reads gào. 道 is dǎo 'to lead, guide' (= 導; Zhu Xi: 去聲); 善 'well, skilfully' is adverbial too. 不可則止 'if it is not possible, then stop'. 毋 wú 'do not'; 自辱 'to disgrace oneself'; 焉 'in it'. Zhu Xi: friends are there to support one's humaneness (12.24), so one gives one's whole heart in telling him and makes one's words good in guiding him; but friends are joined by what is right, so if it does not work one stops — to be pushed away for pressing too often (數, compare 4.26) is to disgrace oneself. He Yan's Bao Xian: 忠告 is telling him what is right and wrong; guide him with goodness; if he does not follow, stop; if one must keep on speaking, one may be insulted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 忠告而以善導之，否則止，無自辱焉 — 'guide him with goodness', 否則 'otherwise' for 不可則, 無 for 毋, and 導, the later graph of 道 'to guide'.

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
君子以文㑹友，
以友輔仁。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said: “The gentleman by letters meets his friends;
by his friends he props up his humaneness.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “The gentleman's friendships are formed over letters, and his friends in turn brace him on the way to humaneness.”
sentences.n: Two clauses in one frame: 以 X + verb + object, 'by X he…'. 文 'letters', the shared study of the texts; 㑹 (the edition's form of 會) 'to meet, gather'; 輔 fǔ 'to support, to prop'. Zhu Xi: in discussing learning one meets friends, and the Way grows clearer; in taking what is good from them to support one's humaneness, virtue advances day by day. He Yan's Kong Anguo: friends are joined by letters and virtue; friends have the way of 'cutting and polishing' one another (切磋, as in the ode of 1.15), and so they help complete one's own humaneness. Master Zeng is the disciple Zeng Shen. With this the book ends.
